passage:
Sunday. First week as head of the fest team. I've swung from one extreme to the other. On Monday I redid Aditi's poster because the font looked off, and she said “oh, okay” in a flat voice. On Wednesday I said nothing when Karan missed the deadline, because I didn't want to be the bossy one. Today the sponsor letter wasn't ready and everyone looked at me. My ears went hot. I realised I'd been trying to prove I could lead instead of asking what the team needed.

Tomorrow: ask everyone what's blocking them, split the letter into two parts, and ask Aditi to explain her font choice.
— Bidisha

qa.q: What did Bidisha redo on Monday?
qa.a: Bidisha redid Aditi's poster because the font looked off.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha say nothing when Karan missed the deadline?
qa.a: Bidisha did not want to be seen as bossy after over-controlling earlier, so avoiding conflict felt safer.

qa.q: What is Bidisha's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: Bidisha plans to ask everyone what is blocking them, split the sponsor letter into two parts and ask Aditi to explain the font choice.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when the poster was redone?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt undervalued and quietly hurt, shown by the flat “oh, okay.”

grounding: A student head of a fest team feels pressure to prove themselves, swings between over-control and avoiding conflict, and refocuses on what the team needs.

passage:
I'm Nirmala, and in my second year I was made head of the college fest hospitality team. Twelve people. I was terrified of looking useless.
So for the first two weeks, I did everything myself. I checked every guest list, rewrote every email, redid Pema's seating chart at midnight. Pema stopped asking me anything.
Then I swung the other way. When two volunteers fought over shifts, I avoided them for three days, hoping it would sort itself out. It didn't.
Finally, our faculty advisor asked me, “Nirmala, what does the team need to make the guests feel welcome?” That changed it. I gave Pema the seating back, fixed the shift roster with the two volunteers, and just kept asking that question.

qa.q: How many people were on the hospitality team?
qa.a: Twelve people.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel at the start of the role?
qa.a: Nirmala felt terrified of looking useless, which led to trying to control everything.

qa.q: What question changed Nirmala's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: "What does the team need to make the guests feel welcome?" It shifted the focus from self-proving to serving the group's goal.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when the seating chart was redone at midnight?
qa.a: Pema probably felt undermined and discouraged, which is why Pema stopped asking anything.

grounding: A student recalls a first leadership role swinging between over-control and avoiding conflict, before learning to serve the group's goal.

passage:
NSS faculty advisor's note, end of September.
Disha became our unit's student head in July. In the first month, she controlled everything: every poster, every message, every visit plan. Volunteers stopped suggesting ideas.
In August she seemed to overcorrect. When Lalit and another volunteer disagreed about the cleanliness drive, she said, “Sort it out between yourselves,” and left the meeting. The drive was nearly cancelled.
This week I asked her what our goal for the village camp was. She paused and said, “That the families actually get the health camp.” She then gave Lalit charge of transport, resolved the disagreement in ten minutes, and let volunteers choose their roles. I'll keep meeting her fortnightly.

qa.q: What did Disha give Lalit charge of?
qa.a: She gave Lalit charge of transport.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt in her first month as head?
qa.a: She was probably anxious to prove herself, which is why she tried to control every poster and message.

qa.q: What helped Disha find a better way to lead?
qa.a: The advisor's question about the goal helped her focus on the families, so she delegated and settled the disagreement quickly.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when Disha left the meeting?
qa.a: Lalit likely felt frustrated and unsupported, left to sort out a disagreement with no help.

grounding: An advisor's note shows a student head swinging between over-control and avoidance before learning that leading means serving the goal.

passage:
Sunday night
I'm the new head of the photography club and I keep getting it wrong.
Week one: I edited everyone's pictures myself because I wanted the exhibition to be perfect. Arnab said, “Then why do you need us?” and didn't come to the next meeting.
Week two: I felt so bad that I stopped saying anything. When the printing was late, I didn't call anyone. When two members argued about the frames, I pretended not to see.
Today the club's senior advisor asked, “What's the exhibition for?” I said, “To show what we see in this city.” She said, “Then let them show it.”
Tomorrow I'll call Arnab and ask him to choose the street section himself.
Lokesh

qa.q: What did Arnab say in week one?
qa.a: He said, "Then why do you need us?"

qa.q: How has Lokesh been feeling about the new role?
qa.a: Lokesh feels frustrated and unsure, first over-controlling, then guilty enough to go silent.

qa.q: What does the advisor's question help Lokesh see?
qa.a: That the exhibition is for the members to show their view of the city, so leading means letting them do it.

qa.q: How might Arnab react to being asked to choose the street section?
qa.a: He might feel valued again and willing to return, since his own work would matter.

grounding: A student writes about a first leadership role, swinging between over-control and avoiding conflict before learning to serve the group's goal.
